A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DICE by the same authors. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original Zephyr and Llama3 alignment experiments, comparisons with other preference optimizers, and length-regularization and experience-replay ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original Arena-Hard evaluations, reward-model comparisons, third-iteration results, and supplementary analyses.

M1.justification: The specified alpha-selection objective changes from the mean absolute pairwise length difference in v1 Eq. (9) to the absolute mean signed length difference in v2 Eq. (6). This is a substantive but localized revision to dataset construction. The reference-policy notation changes equivalently, and the overall DICE procedure remains; the PDFs do not establish whether implementation or existing experiments changed.

E1.justification: Benchmark coverage expands from AlpacaEval 2 to include Arena-Hard's 500 technical problem-solving queries. v2 also evaluates reward-model preference-label agreement with GPT-4o on generated response pairs. UltraFeedback and the two policy backbones remain.

E2.justification: v2 Table 3 adds offline IPO, KTO, and Hinge counterparts, whereas v1 compared their DICE variants against offline DPO. New comparisons also evaluate IntlRM and ERM-555k (Table 5), length-regularized DPO (Table 7), and PPO using implicit rewards (Table 8).

E3.justification: New protocols include Arena-Hard evaluation with Mistral-Large-Instruct-2407 as judge, GPT-4o label agreement on 500 sampled response pairs, and an internal reward model trained on 60k UltraFeedback pairs. Appendix B extends evaluation to a third iteration, while Appendix F alternates AlpacaEval 2 and Arena-Hard as validation/test benchmarks for replay-weight selection. The original main training budget remains.

E4.justification: The original length-weight and replay-ratio ablations remain, including the relocated Llama3 sweep. v2 adds analyses of third-iteration degradation, reward-label fidelity, reward shaping versus loss-based length regularization, PPO use of implicit rewards, and replay-weight selection across benchmarks (Section 4.4 and Appendices B, D, F).

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without confidence intervals. v2 Tables 9 and 10 introduce 95% confidence intervals for Arena-Hard scores. Their estimation procedure and independent training-run counts are not specified, so this establishes additional uncertainty reporting rather than increased repeated experimentation.

E6.justification: The main DICE AlpacaEval 2 LC scores remain 20.71 and 27.55. However, Table 1 swaps the Zephyr LLM-as-a-Judge iteration-1 LC/WR values from 17.81/15.36 to 15.36/17.81. Substantial new results include Arena-Hard scores, reward agreement of 0.698 versus 0.624 for IntlRM and 0.656 for ERM-555k, and third-iteration DICE LC scores of 14.02/20.61. Other new comparator results are added, while Tables 1 and 3 lose average-length entries.

T1.justification: Moving the absolute value outside the expectation in the alpha objective is a mathematical revision, not equivalent notation. Appendix A also explicitly defines optimality using the underlying Bradley-Terry reward and states the single-optimal-response assumption. The earlier on-policy sampling argument and derivations are otherwise retained after relocation from v1 Section 4.1.

C1.justification: The central claim of self-alignment through DPO implicit rewards remains. v2 adds an explicit belief that the approach can improve any DPO-tuned base model and claims competitiveness with scalar rewards trained on the same seed data. The abstract and conclusion emphasize gains across tested backbones; the earlier Gemini superiority claim remains in the results discussion.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning implicit rewards' advantage on their own generated samples, fixed prompts as a possible cause of iteration degradation, backbone quality as an explanation for replay-weight differences, and the length-quality trade-off of regularized DPO. It also qualifies the PPO comparison through tuning-resource limitations. Conversely, v1's specific warning about DICE-IPO length exploitation is removed.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the beta search grid, first-iteration tuning, parameters remaining fixed across iterations, and benchmark selection/transfer procedures. It adds OpenRLHF implementation references, reward-model identifiers, and the regularized-DPO lambda grid. Most existing hardware, generation, training-budget, and code-access information is unchanged; these disclosures do not establish changes to existing runs.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands coverage of iterative alignment with external and internal rewards, adding works such as Dong, Xiong, Ding, Pang, Muldrew, and Furuta. It adds implicit-reward applications to preference-pair selection, distinguishes DICE's outcome rewards from dense-reward approaches, and connects replay to learning from demonstrations. These changes extend research positioning beyond the citation-style conversion.

P1.justification: Related Work moves from Section 2 to Section 6, the on-policy theoretical analysis moves into Appendix A, and the method exposition and appendices are reorganized. The abstract, contribution statements, related-work prose, and conclusion are revised, with terminology standardized from DPO-ed to DPO-tuned. The broader-impact discussion is replaced by a brief ethics statement.

P2.justification: Table 1 replaces average-length columns with Arena-Hard results, and Table 3 becomes a matched offline-versus-DICE comparison. New Tables 5–10 display reward accuracy, additional iterations, alternative methods, and tuning results with confidence intervals. Existing appendix figures are relocated and renumbered, Figure 1's baseline bar is revised, and the document adopts the ICLR layout.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important evidential gaps in v1: Arena-Hard broadens validation, matched offline counterparts make Table 3 more informative, direct reward-label evaluation tests a central premise, and third-iteration results document failure rather than merely mentioning it. Tuning disclosures and cross-benchmark checks further strengthen assessment. Removing some response-length results and the IPO length-exploitation warning reduces transparency, but these losses are outweighed by the substantially stronger comparisons and validation.
